title: Thixoextrusion of AZ91D magnesium alloy: effect of processing parameters on flow behavior and product properties
abstract: Abstract The magnesium alloy AZ91D was investigated to evaluate its microstructural evolution, flow behavior, and mechanical response during semi-solid extrusion (thixoextrusion) in a pilot-scale plant. Prior to extrusion, globular microstructures suitable for semi-solid processing were obtained through partial remelting heat treatment performed at 560 and 575 °C for 10 min. The influence of billet condition, extrusion temperature, and piston speed (3.33–16.66 mm·s –1 ) on extrusion behavior, product integrity, microstructure, and hardness was systematically analysed. The results showed that piston speed is the most influential processing parameter governing material flow and defect formation during thixoextrusion. Sound products were obtained at piston speeds up to 8.33 mm·s –1 , whereas speeds of 10.00 mm·s –1  and above promoted liquid-phase segregation, cracking, and porosity formation. Increasing extrusion temperature reduced the maximum extrusion pressure by increasing the liquid fraction available during processing, while billet conditioning improved semi-solid flowability and microstructural homogeneity. Furthermore, a predictive second-order regression model was developed to estimate the maximum extrusion pressure (Pmax) as a function of the processing parameters, providing a practical tool for process optimization. Microstructural and hardness analyses revealed a clear relationship between local deformation conditions, microstructural heterogeneity, and hardness distribution across the extruded specimens. The results contribute to a better understanding of AZ91D thixoextrusion and provide useful guidelines for the industrial implementation and optimization of semi-solid magnesium alloy processing.
journal: The International Journal of Advanced Manufacturing Technology

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Magnesium (Mg) alloys have attracted considerable attention in recent decades because of their unique combination of low density, high specific strength, and excellent castability, making them among the lightest structural materials available for engineering applications. They have been widely used in the automotive [ 1 ], aerospace [ 2 ], electronics [ 3 ], and biomedical [ 4 ] fields, among others. Despite challenges associated with corrosion resistance and limited formability, ongoing research and alloy development continue to expand the potential applications of Mg-based materials, underscoring their strategic importance in sustainable and advanced lightweight design.

The processing of Mg-based alloys involves a variety of techniques aimed at optimizing their microstructure and enhancing their mechanical properties, with particular emphasis on forming methods because of the limited ductility of these alloys at room temperature [ 5 ]. Conventional forming processes, such as extrusion, rolling, forging, and stamping, are commonly performed at elevated temperatures to improve plasticity through the activation of additional slip systems in the hexagonal close-packed ( hcp ) Mg lattice [ 6 ]. Thermomechanical processing not only enhances formability but also refines grain size, increases strength, and tailors the final properties for specific requirements. Previous studies have demonstrated that processing routes and heat treatments (HT) strongly influence the microstructure, anisotropy, formability, fracture behavior, and mechanical performance of Mg alloys. For example, significant relationships between microstructural evolution and mechanical behavior have been reported for Mg-Li-based alloys subjected to different thermomechanical and HT conditions [ 7 ,  8 ]. In recent years, advanced forming techniques, such as severe plastic deformation and thixoforming, have further broadened the possibilities for manufacturing complex components while maintaining desirable mechanical properties [ 9 ]. Overall, careful control of processing parameters is essential to overcome intrinsic limitations and to fully exploit the lightweight potential of Mg alloys in demanding engineering applications.

The extrusion of Mg alloys presents significant challenges, primarily because of the high initial pressures required and the inherently low extrusion speeds, both of which contribute to increased processing costs. In industrial practice, typical extrusion speeds for low-alloyed Mg grades, such as AZ21, and simple profiles range from 300 to 500 mm·s –1 . However, these speeds may decrease by an order of magnitude or more depending on the alloying content (e.g., AZ61A, AZ80A, ZK60A) and the complexity of the extruded profiles. Furthermore, extruded Mg alloy products are often susceptible to surface defects and may exhibit pronounced anisotropy, which can further limit their performance and applicability [ 10 ]. Hydroforming is a technique that increases processing speed by using fluid pressure to shape the material rather than relying on piston displacement [ 11 ].

As an alternative manufacturing route, thixoextrusion is a semi-solid metal forming process that combines the advantages of casting and forging to shape alloys, particularly non-ferrous metals, such as Mg or Al alloys. In this process, the billet is partially melted to achieve a specific solid-liquid fraction, allowing the material to exhibit thixotropic behavior, which enables easier flow under shear [ 12 ]. The main processing parameters include temperature, which determines the solid fraction; piston speed (ram velocity), which affects flow stress and productivity; and the applied extrusion pressure.

Despite the growing interest in semi-solid processing of Mg alloys, most previous studies have focused on microstructural conditioning routes or on specific thixoforming operations. Comparatively little attention has been devoted to the combined effects of billet condition, extrusion temperature, and piston speed on thixoextrusion performance. Moreover, the relationship among these processing variables, extrusion pressure, defect formation, microstructural evolution, and final mechanical properties remains insufficiently understood for AZ91D alloy. Therefore, the present tudy provides a comprehensive experimental evaluation of AZ91D thixoextrusion under different processing conditions and establishes correlations among process parameters, product integrity, microstructural characteristics, and hardness distribution. Furthermore, a predictive model for maximum extrusion pressure is proposed as a practical tool for process optimization and industrial implementation of AZ91D thixoextrusion.

sections.heading: Materials
paragraphs: Cast billets of AZ91D Mg alloy (Al 8.90  Zn 0.65  Mn 0.20  Si 0.02  Mg bal ., wt%) were supplied by Perfectal S.A., and produced under Ar + 1%SF 6  protective atmosphere to prevent oxidation of the highly reactive molten material [ 13 ]. Figure  1 (a) shows a machined sample, while Fig.  1 (b) presents its corresponding drawing. The cast billets were pre-HTed (445 ± 5 °C for 12 h in an atmosphere of Ar + 1%SF 6 ), followed by air cooling, to homogenize the microstructure of the cast material. Prior to thixoextrusion, the samples were HTed in a Hobersal HCV-125 furnace, reaching and maintaining the samples at 560–575 °C for 10 min and water-quenched. Thes conditions are hereafter designated as HT560 and HT575, respectively. Sample received from the supplier and subjected only to pre-HT are referred to as “No HT”.
Fig. 1 Samples cast and machined for thixoextrusion. ( a ) sample and ( b ) dimensions

sections.heading: Thixoextrusion procedure
paragraphs: Thixoextrusion experiments were carried out at the Pole d’Ingénierie des Matériaux de Wallonie (PiMW) at the Université de Liège (Liège, Belgium). The experimental procedure followed the scheme illustrated in Fig.  2 (a). Each sample was heated in an induction furnace for 3 min before the thixoextrusion. The selected temperature were: 500, 525, 540, and 560 °C, corresponding to AZ91D solid/liquid phase ratios of 0.9, 0.8, 0.7, and 0.5, respectively. These temperatures were selected based on the Mg-Al phase diagram for AZ91D composition, Fig.  3 , which indicates a liquid/solid phase region between 470 and 595 °C. Samples temperatures were monitored using thermocouples. The corresponding solid/liquid fractions were estimated through simulations performed with Keysight ProCAST software to validate the analytical interpretation of phase diagram. Graphite was used as a lubricant during extrusion processing, and the experimental conditions are summarized in Table  1 . The thixoextrusion dies, shown in Fig.  2 (c, d), were manufactured from quenched and tempered DIN 1.2344 steel and designed with an extrusion ratio of 8.5 and an angle of 65º, as illustrated in Fig.  2 (b).
Fig. 2 ( a ) scheme for thixoextrusion of AZ91D samples and thixoextrusion die: ( b ) drawing, ( c ) closed, and ( d ) open dies
Fig. 3 Mg-Al phase diagram, highlighting AZ91D composition. (adapted from [ 14 ]).

The experimental identifiers reported in Table  1  correspond to the original experimental campaign and are retained throughout the manuscript for traceability purposes. The numbering does not represent the chronological sequence of the experiments or any specific processing condition. The experimental campaign was designed as a parametric study rather than a formal Design of Experiments (DoE). The selected processing conditions were chosen to evaluate the influence of the main thixoextrusion variables, namely billet condition, extrusion temperature, and piston speed. The extrusion temperatures were selected within the semi-solid processing range of AZ91D alloy in order to generate different solid-liquid fractions during processing, whereas the piston speeds were chosen according to the operating capabilities of the pilot-scale equipment and to investigate the transition from stable material flow to defect formation. Additional experiments were performed under selected conditions to verify process repeatability and to assess the consistency of the observed trends.

sections.heading: Microstructural and mechanical characterization
paragraphs: For microstructural characterization before and after the thixoextrusion, specimens were prepared for metallographic analysis in accordance with ASTM E3-11 [ 15 ]. The samples were etched using picral reagent and examined by optical microscope (OM) using a Leica MEF4M microscope equipped with QWin software, as well as by scanning electron microscope (SEM) using a Jeol JSM-5600 micrisciope equipped with an energy dispersive X-ray spectrometer (EDS) system. In addition, the hydraulic press pressure was constinuously monitored to its relationship with extrusion temperature and piston speed. Vickers microhardness was performed using a load of 1.96 N applied for 15 s, following ASTM E384-22 [ 16 ]. Five indentations were made for each sample, and the average value was reported.

sections.heading: Billets characteristics
paragraphs: The as-received AZ91D cast billet exhibited a dendritic microstructure composed of primary α-Mg dendrites and interdendritic β-Mg 17 Al 12  phases, as shown in Fig.  4 (a). After the homogenization pre-HT, the microstructure became more homogeneous, consisting of rounded α-Mg grains surrounded by β-Mg 17 Al 12  phase, as observed in Fig.  4 (b). This homogenization pre-HT constitutes an intermediate processing step prior to semi-solid conditioning and differs from processing routes based on direct forming within liquid-solid transition region, such as those reported by Rassili and Atkinson [ 17 ] for steels.

The EDS line-scan analysis presented in Fig.  4 (e) revealed compositional variations within the α-Mg phase. Al content differed between the grain center (α 1 ) and the grain boundary region (α 2 ), with α 2  exhibiting higher Al concentrations as a result of diffusion during the homogenization pre-HT. The β-Mg 17 Al 12  phase exhibited the highest Al content– approx. 35 wt% Al and 6 wt% Zn, whereas the α-Mg matrix contained approx. 8 wt% Al. The dark particles distributed throughout the microstructure were identified by EDS–Figure  4 (f)–analysis as Al 8 (Fe, Mn) 5  precipitates, as shown in Fig.  4 (d).

Fig. 4 Characterization of AZ91D billets prior to semi-solid conditioning: ( a ) OM image of as-cast billet; ( b - c ) OM and ( d ) SEM image of pre-HTed billet with ( e ) EDS line-scan analysis and ( f ) EDS spectrum

Thixoextrusion was done using billets in three different conditions, illustred in Fig.  5 : No HT–Figure  5 (a), HT560 (water-quenched from 560 °C)–Figure  5 (b), and HT575 (water-quenched from 575 °C)–Figure  5 (c). The No HT condition exhibited a smaller grain size than the HTed conditions, which is consistent with the diffusional mechanisms responsible for grain coarsening and grain growth during the HT process. Larger grain sizes are generally associated with higher ductility because of the reduced number of grain boundaries acting as barriers to dislocation motion. Regarding the HT temperatures, both 560–575 °C are sufficiently above the  solvus  temperature to promote a fully solutionized microstructure. However, solutionizing HT at 575 °C provides a greater driving force for the dissolution of any residual β-Mg 17 Al 12  particles, particularly the coarse ones that may persist after the homogeneizing pre-HT processing.
Fig. 5 Microstructure of AZ91D samples before thixoextrusion. ( a ) No HT, ( b ) HT560, and ( c ) HT575

A more detailed interpretation of the microstructural evolution can be established by considering the globularization mechanisms typically observed in semi-solid AZ91D alloy. During heating into the semi-solid temperature range, the interdendritic β-Mg 17 Al 12  phase progressively dissolves and reacts with the the α-Mg matrix, promoting the formation of liquid films along grain boundaries. As the liquid fraction increases, dendrite arms become separated and progressively rounded, leading to the development of a more globular microstructure. Simultaneously, diffusional phenomena contribute to the reduction of surface curvature and interfacial energy, favouring spheroidization of the primary α-Mg phase.

At longer exposure times and higher temperatures, grain coalescence and Ostwald ripening mechanisms may become active, resulting in grain growth and changes in particle morphology [ 18 ]. Consequently, the final microstructure is governed by the balance between dendrite fragmentation, spheroidization, grain coalescence, and liquid-phase formation. These mechanisms explain the differences observed between the No HT, HT560 and HT575 conditions and their subsequent influence on material flow during thixoextrusion.

Previous dimensional characterization performed during the development of the AZ91D semi-solid conditioning route demonstrated that HT promote a significant reduction in grain irregularity and an increase in grain globularity [ 19 ]. Consequently, the HTed billets are expected to exhibit improved semi-solid flowability and a more homogeneous deformation behavior during thixoextrusion compared with the No HT material. The dissolution and redistribution of the β-Mg 17 Al 12  phase during partial remelting are also expected to contribute to a more homogeneous semi-solid microstructure, thereby reducing local stress concentrations and promoting more stable material flow during subsequent thixoextrusion.

Similar relationships between microstructural evolution and mechanical behaviour have been reported for Mg alloys processed through thermomechanical deformation routes. Abd El-Rehim et al. and Mumtaz and Murtaza showed that localized deformation promotes microstructural refinement and recrystallization phenomena, which directly influence hardness and strength through grain boundary strengthening mechanisms. Furthermore, heterogeneous deformation conditions may generate local microstructural variations across the processed section, contributing to differences in mechanical response between the surface and the core of the material [ 20 ,  21 ].

sections.heading: Effect of thixoextrusion processing on the product quality
paragraphs: Samples thixoextruded from different initial billet conditions–No HT, HT560, and HT575–exhibited similar surface quality and overall visual appearance. Figure  6  presents the surface morphology and roughness of the extruded products. For the evaluation of the influence of the initial billet condition, thixoextrusion was carried out at a piston speed of 6.66 mm·s –1  and an extrusion temperature of 560 °C.
Fig. 6 Thixoextrusion of different billets HT. Surface quality

The surface quality assessment presented in Figs.  7  and  8  was conducted qualitatively through the visual inspection of the extruded products. Although no quantitative roughness measurements were conducted, the occurrence of cracks, liquid-phase segregation, and surface discontinuities provides a direct evidence of the influence of processing parameters on product integrity. Therefore, the observations reported herein should be interpreted as comparative indicators of process stability within the investigated processing window. Fig. 7 Aspects of products made with piston speed of (E23) 3.33, (E22) 6.66, (E21) 8.33, and (E24) 16.66 mm·s –1 Fig. 8 E4 sample aspects

A progressive deterioration in surface was observed with increasing piston speed, accompanied by a higher incidence of volumetric defects, including cracks, fratures, and liquid phase segregation. At a piston speed of 16.66 mm·s –1 , the extruded product exhibited extensive cracking, as shown in Fig.  7  (E24). All samples thixoextruded at high piston speeds–10.00–16.66 mm·s –1 –had surface fractures or other significant defects, regardless of the extrusion temperature employed. These observations indicate that piston speed is one of the most influential processing parameters affecting product integrity within the processing window investigated in the present study.

Notably, the transition from sound products to defective specimens occurred consistently when the piston speed exceeded approximately 10 mm·s –1 . All specimens processed at piston speeds of 10.00 and 16.66 mm·s –1  exhibited severe defects or complete failure, whereas all specimens processed at piston speeds equal to or lower than 8.33 mm·s –1  produced sound products. These results suggest the existence of a critical processing threshold beyond which material flow becomes unstable.

Employing a high piston speed–16.66 mm·s –1 –and high temperature–560 °C, a liquid phase segregation was observed at the beginning of the extrusion process, as evidenced by the solidified spread highlighted by a circle in Fig.  8 . This spreading phenomenon, together with the discontinuities seen for high-speed extrusion conditions, can be attributed to the velocity gradient established between the material in contact with the die wall and the material located at the center of the billet cross-section. The material adjacent to the die wall experiences intense friction and undergoes rapid cooling through heat transfer to the extrusion die. As a result, the local liquid fraction decreases, reducing both plasticity and flowability in the peripheral region. In contrast, the central region retains a higher liquid fraction and therefore flows more rapdly. This flow heterogeneity promotes liquid-phase segregation toward the center of the billet and generates internal shear stresses within the semi-solid material. Consequently, volumetric defects, cracks, fractures, and poor surface quality may develop during extrusion.

sections.heading: Microstructural characterization
paragraphs: Flow lines can be observed in the longitudinal sections of the extruded specimens shown in Fig.  9 . Three distinct zones were selected for microstructural analysis, each exhibiting different deformation histories and microstructural characteristics. Zone 0 corresponded to the material located in the die neck region immediately before the extrusion outlet; Zone 1 corresponded to the steady-state extruded material; and Zone 2 corresponded to the first volume of material extruded, located at the sample tip. The purpose of the microstructural analyses presented in Figs.  9 ,  10 ,  11  and  12  was to identify the local microstructural changes generated during thixoextrusion and their relationship with material flow behavior, phase distribution, defect formation, and the mechanical response of the extruded products.
Fig. 9 Sample E7 cross-sectional view for microstructural analysis

The microstructure of Zone 0, presented in Fig.  10 , exhibits elongated grains aligned along the flow path imposed by the die geometry during extrusion. The pronounced curvature in the grain structure near the corner indicates severe plastic deformation, which causes the grains to stretch and bend as they are pushed through the die opening. Such grain alignment is characteristics of extruded metals and is directly related to the directional nature of plastic flow under high pressure and temperature. Figure  10  also reveals dispersed β-Mg 17 Al 12  particles within the α-Mg matrix, visible as darker regions.
Fig. 10 OM of sample E7 Zone 0

Zone 1, represented by the composite of micrographs shown in Fig.  11 , reveals the evolution of the crystallographic texture and grain morphology typically observed in extruded metallic materials, which significantly affects their anisotropic mechanical behavior. The grains, elongated along the extrusion direction, were thinner near the specimen surface than at its center, indicating that the material adjacent to the die wall likely experienced a lower effective temperature than the central region during extrusion. Under E7 thixoextrusion conditions, no cracks or defects were observed in the material; however, increasing the piston speed caused material failure during thixoextrusion, as previously discussed and illustred in Fig.  7 .
Fig. 11 OM of sample E7 Zone 1

Visual examinations of the OM images suggests that the amount of β-Mg 17 Al 12  phase content decreased from Zone 0 to 1. This observation is evidenced by the lower fraction of dark regions visible in Fig.  11  compared with Fig.  10 . The partial remelting associated with heating the alloy into the α-Mg + liquid phase diagram (Fig.  3 ) promotes the dissolution of part of the β-Mg 17 Al 12  phase back into the α-Mg matrix. The degree of dissolution depends on both the processing temperature and the exposure time. Higher temperatures, particularly those closer to the  liquidus , increase the extent of dissolution, while longer holding times promote diffusion-controlled homogenization processes within the solid phase.

Overall, the microstructures presented in Figs.  9 ,  10 ,  11  and  12  demonstrate the strong influence of material flow and local deformation conditions on grain morphology and β-Mg 17 Al 12  phase distribution during thixoextrusion. These microstructural variations help explain the differences in product integrity, defect formation, and hardness distribution observed in the extruded specimens.

The most pronounced microstructural differences were observed in the peripheral region of Zone 1, which corresponds to the area subjected to the highest deformation. For this reason, microstructures obtaines under different processing conditions are compared in Fig.  12 . Comparison of the effects of extrusion temperature piston speed indicates that speed exerts a greater influence on grain morphology than temperature within the investigated processing window. The grains appear more elongated at a piston speed of 6.66 than at 8.33 mm·s⁻¹. This behavior may be related to differences in flow conditions and frictional interactions during extrusion, which influence the local stress distribution. The effect of temperature is mainly reflected in the morphology and distribution of the segregated liquid phase, which appears more pronounced at 560 °C than at 525 °C, as shown in Fig.  12 .
Fig. 12 OM of samples’ surface of Zone 1

Higher magnification SEM images of the porous, presented in Fig.  13 , indicate that the porosity formation mechanism in thixoextruded AZ91D alloy is associated with the resolidification of the liquid phase present during semi-solid processing. Local volumetric contraction may occur during solidification of the liquid phase, generating voids when the resulting shrinkage cannot be fully compensated by the feeding of the remaining or surrounding liquid. Unlike conventional casting shrinkage porosity, the defects observed in the present study appear to be strongly influenced by local liquid-phase segregation and subsequent resolidification during thixoextrusion. High piston speeds promote non-uniform flow behavior between the billet center and the material in contact with the die walls, favoring local accumulation and increasing the likelihood of defect formation.

The spherical morphology of the porosity and the dendritic surface features observed with them, highlighted in Fig.  13 , provide evidence of rapid liquid-solid transformation. Similar features have been reported in rapidly solidified materials, such as gas-atomized powders [ 22 ]. Therefore, reducing piston speed, improving thermal homogeneity within the billet, and carefully controlling the solid fraction during thixoextrusion are expected to minimize liquid segregation and consequently reduce the occurrence of these defects.
Fig. 13 SEM image of porous. Sample E7

Several OM images from Zone 2 were merged in Fig.  14  to illustrate that the microstructural heterogeneity seen between the surface and center of the specimen in Zone 1–Figure  11 –is not present at the extruded tip. In this region, neither a pronounced grain texture nor elongated grains were observed. Nevertheless, it should be noted that the material corresponding to Zone 2 is typically removed and discarded in industrial extrusion applications because of the geometrical irregularities and undesirable microstructures that develop during the initial stage of die filling and material flow stabilization.
Fig. 14 OM of sample E7 Zone 2

Figure  15  shows a cross-section of representative defects observed in a thixoextruded specimen. In sample E4, dark regions can be observed at the initial stage of failure, identified as as zone R1. These dark areas are believed to correspond to regions enriched in the segregated liquid phase, suggesting that they possessed lower mechanical resistance than the surrounding solid material and therefore acted as preferential sites for crack nucleation. Furthermore, a greater elongation and plastic deformation of the grains is observed in the vicinity of the defect, indicating localized deformation associated with the failure process.
Fig. 15 Defect in an AZ91D thixoextruded sample. ( a ) macroscopy and OM imagens of regions ( b ) R2 and ( c ) R1

sections.heading: Effect of thixoextrusion parameters on material’s hardness
paragraphs: Figure  16  ilustrates the hardness evolution of extruded AZ91D alloy samples under different processing conditions. The thixoextrusion parameters influenced the mechanical properties of the material, with all samples exhibiting a clear hardness gradient from the sampleto the center, the late consistently presenting lower hardness values. Among the samples seen in Fig.  16 , sample E3 (extrusion temperature of 560 °C and piston speed of 8.33 mm·s –1 ) exhibited the largest hardness gradient between the surface and the center. This behavior can be attributed to the higher piston speed, which promoted greater microstructural differences across the cross-section as a result of increased liquid-phase segregation and, consequently, greater microstructural heterogeneity. As previously discussed and illustrated in Figs.  10  and  11 , the peripheral region experienced more intense deformation than the central region, ontrbutng to the observed hardness variation.
Fig. 16 Hardness of AZ91D thixoextruded samples

The hardness distribution observed across the extruded samples can be interpreted in terms of the local microstructural variations generated during semi-solid deformation. The outer regions of the extruded billets experienced higher deformation levels because of frictional interaction with the die walls and the resulting shear stresses. This condition promoted grain elongation, increased dislocation density, and enhanced strain hardening, leading to higher hardness values near the surface. In contrast, the central region contained a greater proportion of segregated liquid during extrusion and underwent lower effective deformation, resulting in lower hardness values.

Furthermore, the partial dissolution of the β-Mg 17 Al 12  phase during heating and its subsequent redistribution during cooling contributed to local variations in strengthening. Therefore, the measured hardness gradients are consistent with the microstructural heterogeneity observed between the surface and the core of the extruded specimens. These results confirm that extrusion parameters influence not only material flow behavior but also the final mechanical response through their effect on microstructural evolution.

The hardness values obtained in the present study can be compared with values reported in the literature for AZ91D alloy processed under different conditions. Reported hardness values include approx. 74 HV [ 23 ] for cast condition; 55 [ 24 ], and 83 HV [ 25 ] for cast billets; 91 HV [ 26 ] after friction stir processing, and 82 HV [ 27 ] for thixoextruded material. These results demonstratethat the mechanical properties of AZ91D are highly dependent on both the processing technique and parameters. In addition, HT also play a significant role, as demonstrated by Yang, Wei, and Hou [ 27 ], who reported that aging at 216 °C for tens of hours increased the hardness of AZ91D from 57 to 85 HV because of β-Mg 17 Al 12  phase precipitation.

A similar precipitation response is expected in HTed thixoextruded AZ91D. During aging, β-Mg 17 Al 12  precipitates are expected to form along the grain boundaries and within the grains as a consequence of the supersaturated Al retained in the α-Mg matrix after extrusion. Compared with the as-cast AZ91D microstructure shown in Fig.  4 (a), the extruded material exhibited a finer and more homogeneous microstructure, characterized by elongated grains and a higher dislocation density due to the severe plastic deformation during extrusion. This microstructural refinement and the associated stored strain energy are expected to promote a faster and more homogeneous nucleation of the β-Mg 17 Al 12  during aging, potentially enhancing the age-hardening response and improving mechanical properties such as strength and creep resistance. In contrast, cast AZ91D, with a coarser dendritic structure and lower dislocation density, may result in slower precipitation kinetics and a less uniform β-Mg 17 Al 12  precipitates distribution, thereby reducing strengthening efficiency.

Although texture evolution was not evaluated in the present work, crystallographic texture is known to significantly influence the mechanical behavior and anisotropy of Mg alloys. Therefore, the hardness variations discussed herein should be interpreted primarily in terms of the observed microstructural heterogeneity and local deformation conditions. Future work should include electron backscattered diffraction (EBSD) [ 28 ] or high-energy X-ray diffraction (HEXRD) [ 29 ] texture characterization to complement the microstructural and hardness analyses presented in this study.

sections.heading: Effect processing parameters on extrusion pressure
paragraphs: Figure  17  presents the pressure evolution during thixoextrusion of billets with different initial conditions: No HT, HT560, and HT575. The pressure–time curves exhibited similar initial slopes for all conditions. However, the HTed billets showed a distinct pressure peak before reaching a steady-state pressure plateau, whereas the No HT specimen reached the plateau without a pronounced pressure peak. This behavior may be associated with the microstructural changes induced by solution HT and quenching. The HTed billets exhibited a more homogeneous and solutionized microstructure than the untreated material, which may have increased the resistance to deformation during the initial stages of extrusion, resulting in a higher peak pressure.
Fig. 17 Extrusion pressure versus displacement with different billets HT

As shown in Fig.  18 , increasing the piston speed resulted in a reduction in the extrusion pressure. During the initial stage of ram displacement, relatively low pressure was required because only a small volume of material was subjected to deformation. As extrusion progressed and a large volume of material was forced through the die, the required load increase, resulting in a corresponding increase in hydraulic pressure to maintain the prescribed speed. Fig. 18 Extrusion pressure versus displacement with different ( a ) velocities and ( b ) temperatures

At lower speed–3.33–6.66 mm·s –1 –the coefficient of friction between the specimen and die walls contributed to an increase in the required extrusion pressure. In contrast, at higher piston speed–16.66 mm·s –1 –the pressure decreased. Another factor the may contribute to this behavior is the segregation of the liquid phase during the semi-solid flow, which promotes non-uniform deformation. This effect is particularly evident in the pressure curve corresponding to a piston speed of 16.66 mm·s –1 , which exhibites luctuations characterized by successive peaks and valleys rather than the smooth pressure evolution observed at lower piston speeds. These pressure oscillations provide additional evidence of flow instability and defect formation during thixoextrusion and are consistent with the fractures observed in specimen E24–Figure  7  (E24).

The influence of piston speed on product quality was also evident from the surface integrity analyses. Although higher piston speeds reduced the required extrusion pressure, they promoted liquid-phase segragation and increased occurrence of defects, as observed in HTed at 575 °C and thixoextruded at 525 °C–Figure  7 . These results indicate a trade-off between minimizing extrusion load and maintaining product integrity.

A regression analysis was performed using the experimental results obtained from defect-free specimens, i.e., samples processed at piston speeds lower than 10 mm·s –1 , to establish a predictive relationship between the maximum extrusion pressure and the main thixoextrusion parameters. The billet condition, extrusion temperature, and piston speed were initially evaluated. However, the influence of billet condition on the maximum extrusion pressure was found to be considerably lower than the effects of extrusion temperature and piston speed. Consequently, only extrusion temperature and piston speed were retained in the final regression model.

The regression model indicates that the maximum extrusion pressure increases as both piston speed and extrusion temperature decrease. Furthermore, the quadratic terms associated with piston speed and extrusion temperature exhibited only a limited influence on the response surface, as illustrated on Fig.  19 . Fig. 19 Graph for the mathematical model for extrusion pressure versus piston speed and thixoextrusion temperature

The experimental results consistently demonstrated that piston speed exerted a stronger influence on the maximum extrusion pressure than extrusion temperature. In addition, the processing conditions associated with lower extrusion pressures generally coincided with increased liquid-phase segregation and a higher tendency for defect formation, indicating a trade-off between reducing extrusion load and maintaining product integrity.

Among the investigated process parameters, piston speed had the most significant effect on the required pressure. At lower temperatures, reducing the piston speed from 8.33 to 3.33 mm·s⁻¹ increased the pressure from approx. 400 to 1100 MPa. In contrast, at higher temperatures, the same speed reduction increased extrusion pressure from approx. 400 to 600 MPa. These results indicate that, at elevated temperatures, extrusion pressure is predominantly governed by piston speed, whereas at lower temperatures, the combined effect of speed and temperature become more pronounced. Moreover, within the temperature range of 535–560 °C, the extrusion pressure remains consistently more sensitive to changes in piston speed than to variations in temperature, regardless of the speed setting.

A comparison between the experimental and predicted values, presented in Fig.  20 , demonstrates that calculated pressures fall within the range of the experimental values. Therefore, the proposed model provides a satisfactory prediction of the maximum extrusion pressure within the experimental processing window investigated in this study. Furthermore, the absence of systematic pressure differences among the No HT, HT560, and HT575 consitions supports the conclusion that the billet condition has only a minor influence on extrusion pressure compared with extrusion temperature and piston speed.
Fig. 20 Graph for comparison of extrusion pressure obtained by experimental and model

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: The results obtained from the thixoextrusion of AZ91D Mg alloy under different billet conditions, extrusion temperatures, and piston speeds allow the following conclusions to be drawn:

Partial-remelting HT successfully produce microstructures suitable for semi-solid processing. Although, billet condition had a limited effect on the maximum extrusion pressure, it influenced material flow behavior during thixoextrusion and contributed to the microstructural characteristics of the extruded products; Extrusion temperature significantly affects the liquid-to-solid ratio of the semi-solid alloy. Increasing the processing temperature increased the liquid fraction and reduced the maximum extrusion pressure required for material deformation; Piston speed is identified as the most influential processing parameter affecting product integrity. High piston speeds (≥ 10 mm·s –1  under the conditions presented in this study) promoted liquid-phase segregation and flow instability, resulting in resulting in non-uniform deformation between the billet center and the material adjacent to the die walls. This behavior increased the likelihood of defect formation and, in severe cases, led to product failure; Microstructural analyses indicated that the defects detected in the extruded products were associated with localized liquid-phase segregation and subsequent resolidification phenomena during semi-solid deformation. Therefore, reducing piston speed and improving process stability are therefore essential to minimize defect formation; Hardness measurements revealed a clear gradient between the surface and the center of the extruded specimens, with higher hardness values consistently observed near the surface. This behavior was attributed to differences in local deformation conditions, microstructural heterogeneity, and liquid-phase distribution developed during thixoextrusion; A second-order regression model predicts the maximum extrusion pressure as a function of extrusion temperature and piston speed.
